tooltips.optimizer: Adam for ResNet (proven fine-tuning baseline). AdamW for ConvNeXt and DINOv2 — decoupled weight decay prevents overfitting on small datasets.
tooltips.learning_rate: Fine-tuning LR from the model registry. ResNet: 0.001 (standard), ConvNeXt: 0.0001 (LayerNorm is sensitive to large gradients), DINOv2: 0.0002 (LoRA adapter).
tooltips.weight_decay: L2 regularization strength. 0 for ResNet (BatchNorm provides implicit regularization), 0.05 for ConvNeXt (ConvNeXt paper recipe), 0.01 for DINOv2 (light regularization on LoRA adapters).
tooltips.patience: Stops training after 15 consecutive epochs without val_loss improvement. Catches convergence without premature stopping.
tooltips.batch_size: Physical batch=8 (fits 4GB VRAM). Effective batch=32 via gradient accumulation (4 steps). Mathematically identical to batch=32 for cross-entropy loss.
tooltips.epochs: Maximum training duration. Early stopping terminates earlier via patience.
tooltips.test_accuracy: Overall fraction of correctly classified test images (300 total, 50 per class).
tooltips.f1_macro: Harmonic mean of per-class F1 scores. Preferred over accuracy for imbalanced datasets.

research.hero_title: Ultra-Fine-Grained Classification and Open-Set Recognition of Ophrys Orchids
research.hero_university: University of Naples Federico II — DIETI — Master's Degree in Computer Science
research.intro_p1_mid: includes over 300 species of European orchids characterized by an extraordinary morphological similarity that makes their taxonomic identification extremely complex even for expert botanists. This difficulty, known as ultra-fine-grained classification (UFGVC)
research.intro_p1_after: , represents a significant challenge for computer vision systems.
research.intro_p2_before: This thesis addresses the problem by systematically comparing six architectures (ResNet, ConvNeXt, DINOv2) across three learning paradigms: cross-entropy, supervised contrastive learning (SupCon)
research.contrib_1: Multi-architecture benchmark across three learning paradigms
research.contrib_2: Curated dataset: 2,192 training images and 300 test images for the 256×512 architectures (2,232 for 224×224), 6 species with MD5 clean split, and O. garganica used as the hidden novel class for open-set evaluation
research.contrib_3: Latent space analysis via t-SNE projections
research.contrib_4: Open-set evaluation with Mahalanobis, KNN, and Energy techniques
research.dataset_caption: Image distribution per species in training and test splits. O. garganica is in training for Exp 6–8 and excluded from training in Exp 9, where it is reserved for testing as the novel class.
research.dataset_intro: The dataset comprises images of six taxonomic entities of the O. sphegodes complex, all photographed in Italian territory, mainly in Apulia and on the Gargano. Images come from two sources: field photographs taken by the researchers constitute the primary source for O. majellensis and O. sphegodes Palena (species with no counterpart in databases); images collected from open internet databases cover the four most common species: O. exaltata, O. garganica, O. incubacea and O. sphegodes.
research.dataset_callout_leakage: In the initial phases (Exp 1–5), the dataset presented a critical data leakage problem: visually identical images appeared in both training and test sets under different filenames. The discovery was made via MD5 content hashing. Starting from Exp 6, the dataset was cleaned using a three-phase protocol: (1) MD5 deduplication, (2) extraction of a balanced hold-out of 50 images per class, (3) stratified 5-fold cross-validation with seed 57. This clean split forms the basis of all experiments.
research.dataset_callout_novel: O. garganica, recognized as a distinct entity of the O. sphegodes complex, is excluded from training in Exp 9 and reserved exclusively for the test set as a novel class never seen during training. Its taxonomic relevance makes it a challenging case study for evaluating known/novel separability at ultra-fine granularity.
research.dataset_preprocessing: Raw images are processed by a pre-trained Faster R-CNN object detection module that automatically crops the flower by removing the background. Letterbox resize preserves the original aspect ratio with black padding. Input sizes are architecture-native: 256×512 for ResNet, 224×224 for ConvNeXt and DINOv2. During cross-validation, minority classes are oversampled through augmentations (rotations, flip, color jitter, cutout).
research.sect_exp9: Exp 9 — SpHOR with Hidden Novel Class
research.metodo_disegno_intro: The experiments are organized into five series, each adding methodological complexity to the previous one, in a path from closed classification to the open world:
research.metodo_exp6: all architectures are trained with CE loss for 150 epochs with early stopping (patience 15). Establishes the closed-set performance baseline.
research.metodo_exp7: introduces two-phase training. Phase 1: backbone + projection head (128-dim) trained with SupConLoss (τ=0.07) for 100 epochs, validated with 1-NN accuracy. Phase 2: frozen backbone, linear classifier trained with CE for 50 epochs.
research.metodo_exp8: like Exp 7 but with learnable L2-normalized prototypes on the unit sphere and orthogonal repulsion loss (λ=0.01). At test time, four OSR detectors (Mahalanobis, KNN, Energy, Ensemble) determine whether a sample is known or novel.
research.metodo_exp9: identical to Exp 8 but with O. garganica excluded from training: five known classes, garganica reserved for testing as the novel class for OSR and NCD evaluation.
research.metodo_validazione: All experiments use stratified 5-fold cross-validation with seed 57. The main metric for closed-set classification is macro F1, robust to the natural class imbalance (152 images for O. majellensis vs 563 for O. garganica). For open-set, AUROC and the detection rate at 10% FPR are used: the rejection threshold is calibrated so that only 10% of novel images are erroneously accepted, and one measures how many known samples are correctly recognized.
research.metodo_pipeline_osr: For OSR evaluation, the model trained on five known classes is tested on a set that includes O. garganica as the unknown class. The procedure consists of three phases: (1) embedding extraction from training and test sets via a frozen backbone; (2) training of four detectors (Mahalanobis, KNN, Energy, Ensemble) on known embeddings only; (3) computation of AUROC and detection rate at 10% FPR.
research.metodo_arch_fig_caption: Diagram of the training and evaluation pipeline: from image collection to result publication.
research.metodo_osr_flow_caption: Open-Set Recognition pipeline: embedding extraction, detector training, novelty detection. The detectors evaluate the distance/probability that a sample belongs to a known class.

research.contesto_p1_after: (Orchidaceae) includes terrestrial orchids widespread throughout the Mediterranean basin. The plants are perennial, with basal rosette leaves and a flowering stem producing 2 to 12 flowers. Each flower is characterized by a large velvety labellum that constitutes the most conspicuous and diagnostic morphological element.
research.contesto_p2_mid: are known for their pollination system based on sexual mimicry (pseudocopulation)
research.contesto_p2_after: . Each species produces a unique blend of allomones that mimics the sex pheromone of a specific pollinator species. The labellum, in shape, color, and texture, visually mimics the female insect's body; the speculum — a reflective spot on the labellum — simulates light reflected from wings. Only about 10% of flowers are actually pollinated, but each produces up to 12,000 seeds.
research.contesto_p3_mid1: is one of the most taxonomically controversial groups in the plant kingdom
research.contesto_p3_mid2: . Estimates of the number of species vary dramatically: from about 20 (
research.contesto_p3_mid3: , 1980) to over 130 (Delforge, 1995). Frequent hybridization produces over 250 described natural hybrids, and molecular studies have revealed heterogeneous copies of ribosomal ITS DNA in single individuals. The
research.contesto_p3_mid4: complex (the "forretterelle") is one of the most variable groups, with at least 18 subspecific taxa.
research.contesto_p4_before: Our dataset adopts an intermediate classification, treating six entities —
research.contesto_p4_after: — as distinct species, consistent with the Italian taxonomic tradition. The Gargano peninsula constitutes a diversity hotspot for the complex.
research.arch_before: Six architectures from three families were selected to cover the state of the art in visual classification. Classic convolutional networks
research.arch_mid3: were chosen as baselines for computational efficiency. Modernized CNNs
research.arch_mid6: incorporate Transformer design choices (7×7 kernel, Layer Normalization, GELU). The Vision Transformers
research.arch_after: are pre-trained in a self-supervised manner on 142 million images.
research.exp6_p1_before: Exp 6 establishes the closed-set classification baseline with standard CE loss. The softmax objective separates classes with decision hyperplanes but does not structure the latent space: two samples of the same species can project into arbitrary regions of space, as long as the classifier assigns them to the correct class. This lack of structure is acceptable for closed-set classification but becomes critical in open-world scenarios
research.exp6_fig_caption: Training and validation curves for DINOv2-Base in Exp 6 (CE). Stable convergence around 60 epochs, early stopping at 75.
research.exp7_p1_before: To address the structural limitation of CE, Supervised Contrastive Learning (SupCon) is adopted
research.exp7_p1_after: . The SupCon loss explicitly attracts samples of the same class and repels those of different classes in L2-normalized space. The result is a metric space where cosine distance reflects semantic similarity — an essential property for open-set recognition and novel class discovery
research.exp7_fig2_caption: Per-species F1 for the best model of each experiment (Exp 6: ResNet-50, Exp 7: DINOv2-Small, Exp 8: ConvNeXt-Tiny). O. sphegodes is systematically the most difficult species; O. sphegodes Palena and O. majellensis are the easiest.
research.exp7_fig3_caption: Training and validation curves for DINOv2-Small during SupCon training.
research.benchmark_intro: The following table consolidates the performance of all architectures across the experiments, for closed-set classification (test F1) and open-set (AUROC at 10% FPR).
research.futuri_li1: Dataset expansion via citizen science and generative AI.
research.futuri_li3: Systematic integration of XAI with validation by expert botanists.
research.futuri_li4: Field validation through deployment of the OrchID OSR application.
research.risultati_li1_mid: + SupCon (test F1 0.936) — the best among contrastive paradigms.
research.risultati_li2_mid: + SpHOR (AUROC 0.875, novel O. garganica) — demonstration that OSR is achievable in ultra-FGVC.
research.risultati_li3: Open-set recognition goes from a failure with SupCon (known accuracy 0.0) to AUROC 0.875 with SpHOR in Exp 9.
research.risultati_li4: Unsupervised clustering recovers species for high-capacity models, confirming the quality of the SpHOR metric space.
research.risultati_li5: Unsupervised clustering recovers species for high-capacity models (NMI up to 0.84 in Exp 9).
research.exp6_training: All six architectures were trained for a maximum of 150 epochs with patience 15 for early stopping, using the recipes defined in the configuration table.
research.exp6_risultati_before: The table reports the F1 scores. ResNet-50 reaches the highest test F1 (0.980), followed by ResNet-18 (0.978) and DINOv2-Base (0.975): 11–25M parameters suffice to capture the variance of the six species with 2,192 training images. ConvNeXt models remain lower (0.821 and 0.793), with a wide CV-test gap for ConvNeXt-Small (+0.266) indicating high fold variance. DINOv2-Small (0.970) and DINOv2-Base (0.975) confirm the effectiveness of large-scale self-supervised pretraining. The CV-test gap is positive for all models: stratified CV on imbalanced classes tends to underestimate generalization, a pattern consistent with the
research.exp6_risultati_mid: phenomenon: with approximately 2,200 training samples, ResNets (11–25M parameters) operate in the over-parameterized regime where generalization improves with model size, while ConvNeXt-Small (50M parameters) lies closer to the interpolation threshold where overfitting is more severe.
research.exp6_risultati_after: The gap tends to increase with model parameters for the ConvNeXt and DINOv2 families, while ResNets show stable or positive generalization thanks to the implicit regularization of batch normalization.
research.exp6_embedding: The t-SNE projection of DINOv2-Small embeddings reveals that CE produces a poorly structured latent space. Although species are approximately separable, considerable overlap is observed between morphologically similar taxa — particularly between O. sphegodes and O. garganica, which belong to the same taxonomic complex. This lack of geometric structure is intrinsic to the softmax objective: the model has no incentive to organize the latent space beyond what is necessary for classification, producing representations inadequate for open-set recognition. The cosine silhouette score confirms this quantitatively: ResNet-18 achieves 0.664 (CE), while contrastive models (SupCon, SpHOR) show near-zero or negative values, indicating modest cluster separation in the L2-normalized space.
research.exp6_fig_cv_gap: Generalization gap (Test F1 − CV F1) as a function of model parameters. Positive values indicate the model generalizes beyond the cross-validation estimate; negative values indicate overfitting. Modern architectures (ConvNeXt, DINOv2) show larger gaps than ResNets, consistent with the double descent phenomenon.
research.exp7_protocollo: A two-phase training procedure was employed. In Phase 1, the backbone and a projection head (embedding dimension → 128) were trained using the SupCon loss with temperature τ = 0.07. Validation was performed via 1-nearest neighbor accuracy on frozen backbone embeddings. In Phase 2, the projection head was removed and a linear classifier was trained on the frozen backbone using cross-entropy for 50 epochs. Freezing the backbone in Phase 2 is a fundamental methodological choice: it preserves the metric structure of the embedding space, preventing the classifier from distorting representations to maximize closed-set accuracy at the expense of open-set separability.
research.exp7_risultati: The table presents the results. DINOv2-Base achieved the highest test F1 (0.936) with a minimal CV-test gap (+0.004). However, DINOv2-Small shows the best F1-to-parameters ratio (21M params, 0.888 test F1, gap −0.026). At the species level, DINOv2-Small excels on O. sphegodes Palena (F1 = 0.990) and O. majellensis (F1 = 0.990), while the most difficult species remains O. sphegodes (F1 = 0.784), consistent with its high intra-specific phenotypic variability. A notable finding is that large ConvNeXt models (Small) and ResNets underperform in the SupCon setting, suggesting that contrastive learning benefits more from the representational quality of the backbone than from raw capacity.
research.exp7_overfitting_detail: ConvNeXt-Small shows the largest negative CV-test gap (−0.187), confirming that larger CNN architectures tend to overfit in low-data regimes when fine-tuned end-to-end. DINOv2-Base, by contrast, maintains a slightly positive gap (+0.004), reflecting the benefits of large-scale self-supervised pretraining. ResNet-50 shows a positive gap (+0.083), a pattern consistent with double descent and the implicit regularization of batch normalization layers that modern architectures (LayerNorm, GELU) lack.
research.exp7_embedding_osr: The t-SNE projection shows that SupCon produces markedly more cohesive clusters than CE. Intra-class variance is reduced and inter-class separation is improved, particularly for the most distinctive species (O. exaltata, O. incubacea). However, an open-set evaluation reveals a critical limitation: the detector showed 0.0 accuracy on known classes at all thresholds, classifying all inputs as unknown. The mean AUROC was 0.485 (near chance). This indicates that although SupCon produces well-separated class clusters, the distances between clusters are not significantly larger than intra-cluster distances — a fundamental limitation when inter-class morphological differences are as subtle as they are in ultra-fine-grained domains. The embedding space lacks the angular margin needed to distinguish "familiar but unseen" from "truly novel."
research.exp8_motivazione_before: The failure of SupCon-based OSR detection motivated the adoption of Spherical Orthogonal Prototypes (SpHOR)
research.exp8_motivazione_mid: . SpHOR extends contrastive learning by introducing learnable L2-normalized prototypes on the unit sphere — one per class. An orthogonal repulsion loss encourages prototypes to be maximally separated. The orthogonal prototypes partition the unit sphere into conical regions, each occupied by a single species. At inference time, four detectors evaluate whether a sample belongs to a known class: Mahalanobis distance
research.exp8_motivazione_after: from the nearest prototype, K-nearest neighbors (k=5), Energy score
research.exp8_motivazione_end: , and an Ensemble that combines them via normalized averaging.
research.exp8_closedset: The table reports closed-set metrics. Compared to the previous version of the study, the protocol was cleaned up: hard negative mining was disabled, embeddings L2-normalized before the linear head, and the dataset realigned to the current manifest. The result is a systematic improvement: ConvNeXt-Tiny reaches test F1 0.911 and DINOv2-Base 0.910, while the ResNets remain lower (0.560 and 0.750) due to their limited capacity to support the spherical prototype structure.
research.exp8_species: The per-species F1 breakdown reveals a coherent pattern for modern architectures. O. sphegodes — the most phenotypically variable taxon — is the most penalized species (F1 0.80–0.82 for ConvNeXt-Tiny and DINOv2-Base). Conversely, O. sphegodes Palena and O. majellensis reach F1 0.94–0.98, being the most distinctive taxa. O. exaltata and O. garganica show intermediate F1 (0.88–0.90). For the ResNets the pattern is more marked: O. garganica suffers the severest drop (F1 0.22 for ResNet-18, 0.60 for ResNet-50), being the class most sensitive to the limited discriminative capacity of the smaller architectures.
research.exp9_motivazione: Exp 9 is identical to Exp 8 in protocol (SupCon + SpHOR, two phases), but O. garganica is excluded from training, leaving five known classes. The model is evaluated on the test set that includes the hidden novel class, measuring open-set recognition: four detectors (Mahalanobis, KNN, Energy, Ensemble) determine whether a sample belongs to a known class or should be classified as unknown.
research.exp9_caption: Exp 9 — Closed-set F1 on five known classes, AUROC and Detection Rate on the novel class.
research.exp9_osr_intro: The OSR evaluation with O. garganica as the hidden novel class yields positive and consistent results across several architectures:
research.exp9_osr_dinov2b: DINOv2-Base reaches the best AUROC (0.875) with the Ensemble detector, confirming that the Vision Transformer representations, combined with orthogonal prototypes, effectively encode the notion of novelty.
research.exp9_osr_convnext: ConvNeXt-Tiny reaches AUROC 0.850 and the best detection rate at 10% FPR (0.640): the most balanced configuration between closed-set precision and open-set robustness.
research.exp9_osr_resnet: ResNet-18 remains weak (AUROC 0.507): the limited backbone capacity does not support the geometric structure required for OSR.
research.exp9_osr_ensemble: The Ensemble is the most robust detector, being the best for the three most performant configurations (DINOv2-Base, ConvNeXt-Tiny, ConvNeXt-Small).
research.exp9_osr_auroc_caption: OSR AUROC per architecture in Exp 9 with O. garganica as the novel class (best detector per architecture). DINOv2-Base (0.875) and ConvNeXt-Tiny (0.850) clearly exceed the chance level (0.5); ResNet-18 remains the weakest (0.507).
research.exp9_clustering: Unsupervised clustering on Exp 9 embeddings recovers species for high-capacity models: K-means at the true number of classes (six: five known + the novel) reaches NMI 0.844 (ConvNeXt-Tiny), 0.828 (DINOv2-Small), and 0.756 (DINOv2-Base). Weaker architectures recover the structure only partially.
research.exp9_tsne_novel_caption: t-SNE projection of Exp 9 embeddings for DINOv2-Base: the five known species (circles) are well separated, while the novel class O. garganica (crosses) sits at the margins of the known clusters, remaining detectable by the open-set detectors.
research.sintesi_implicazioni: This study demonstrates that open-set recognition is achievable at ultra-fine granularity: with O. garganica excluded from training, DINOv2-Base with SpHOR reaches AUROC 0.875 in Exp 9, clearly exceeding the chance level (0.5). Cross-entropy and SupCon alone are instead insufficient for open-world scenarios: CE does not structure the latent space and the SupCon detector fails (known accuracy 0.0). Spherical orthogonal prototypes provide the necessary regularization. Unsupervised clustering recovers species when the metric space is stable (NMI up to 0.84 in Exp 9). Confusion matrices reveal systematic patterns: the O. exaltata → O. sphegodes pair is the most frequent error (16–20% in Exp 8), consistent with the taxonomy of the O. sphegodes complex, where species share overlapping morphological traits.
research.sintesi_necessita: Discovering new Ophrys species from visual data alone would require additional cues — geographic context, phenological information, or part-based anatomical correspondence as proposed by recent methods such as APL and PartGCD. These methods decompose the visual representation into anatomical parts (labellum, gynostemium, sepals) and align them across species, potentially capturing the fine-grained diagnostic characters that taxonomists use.
research.sintesi_limitazioni: Several limitations should be acknowledged. The open-set evaluation was conducted with a single novel species (O. garganica), belonging to the same taxonomic complex as the known classes. AUROC values are reported without confidence intervals or significance tests. The results of Exp 8 and Exp 9 were obtained in full fine-tuning on a local T2000 GPU. All experiments were conducted on a single dataset with limited geographic coverage (primarily Apulia and Gargano); generalizability to other Mediterranean populations is not guaranteed. Furthermore, the mixed provenance of images (field vs internet photos) introduces a potential domain bias, although all six species have field photos and only four have internet photos. The confusion patterns follow the taxonomy of the complex — O. exaltata ↔ O. sphegodes (16–28%) — indicating that the model learns genuine morphological traits rather than mere domain shortcuts.
